text: Hey, everybody.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like Harrison said, I'm Ben.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm the product manager.

text: I work on our product engine, which is our agent for agent engineering.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What I want to do today is walk you through the process that we have at LangChain of developing and improving our agents through engine, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This agent for engineering, agent engineering, I should say.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, the process of building agents we're very familiar with, it's very challenging.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Everything from the identification of errors as you manually look through traces, as you try to cluster them together based on the different problems that you identify, this kind of root cause analysis for those problems, the spinning up of fixes, the writing of evals, this entire process from start to finish can be very challenging.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so what we've built in Engine is a product and a tool
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: that handles each step of this process, that works to identify the different issues that you might find within your traces, that creates deployable fixes for each one of those identified issues, creates ready-to-use evals for you to run offline and ensure that these fixes work appropriately without regressing, and additional regression detection for any of the issues that might crop back up again after you've attempted to fix them previously.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we're really excited about Engine.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We launched it in May at our Interrupt in San Francisco.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And since then, Engine has scanned over 70 million traces and has created over 21,000 issues for the many customers that are using it today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We're really excited about this progress, but we've had a lot of time and a lot of effort spent on making Engine much better than the version that we released in May as our public beta.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so like I said, the hope of today's little talk and session that I have is I want to walk you through this process that our team has followed for making Engine better and for making this a product that is faster, stronger, cheaper, and go beyond what we have today within this existing agent development lifecycle and what's automated today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The number one thing that I want to talk about actually is the process for evaluating Engine.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As we have been building this very complex agent, it's been very hard to create these evals for Engine as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the reason that it's so hard for Engine is because of the many complex tasks that are handled by this agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so to run you through some of the tasks that are handled, Engine will identify these offending or problematic traces and cluster them together after identifying a root cause.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It will write a readable issue description for a human to read through and parse.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It will investigate that issue and compare the traces to the actual source code of your agent to create a fix.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It will create dataset examples using the offending inputs that it found in production and by creating these ground truth reference outputs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It will monitor for regressions to ensure that this problem doesn't happen again.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so I'm running through all these different stages of this agent and the work that it does.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And each one of these tasks is very different from the last.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so in order for us to ensure that engine performs well and that we can make it better and cheaper, we need to be evaluating these separately.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we have created unique benchmarks for each one of these tasks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so, for example, we have created a unique benchmark for identifying these offending traces that allows us to test engine and understand how well is it able to identify problematic traces.

text: And so in order for us to assess this adequately, the benchmark that we've generated
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: is a set of traces with seeded problems within them.

text: And so it's like finding a needle in a haystack of traces.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we just test engine's ability to find these problematic traces.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now that benchmark is separate from
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Another one that's very similar, which is Engine's ability to cluster those traces by root cause.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For this benchmark, we provide Engine, the agent, with a set of known error traces, as well as a series of existing issues.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we evaluate Engine's ability to match these known error traces to the set of issues or to create new issues.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so these are just a couple of the benchmarks that we've generated.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But like I said, for each one of these various tasks, we have to create new benchmarks and ensure that Engine is performing and is firing on all cylinders for each one of these different tasks that it handles.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so something interesting that I want to highlight as we talk about these benchmarks is that there are two sides to this coin, where we have evals that we need to ensure these benchmarks that we've created that help us to test very specific components of the agent's run.

text: But we also want to ensure that those benchmarks are faithful to what we would see in a production environment, which is the other side of that coin.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so in order to ensure that any of the changes that we find very effective against our benchmarks really are effective in a production environment, we dogfood engine.

text: We try our own products a lot.

text: And we have many different agents that we build at LangChain, including go-to-market agents that handle a bunch of go-to-market-related tasks, like sending outbound, doing prospect research.

text: We can investigate them.

text: The teams that are working on these go-to-market agents or the coding agents can tell us that Engine has found really valuable issues or something is wrong with this description.

text: And it really helps us to balance out
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This process that we have had on the benchmarking and the evaluating of Engine on these specific tasks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But maybe the most interesting of this dogfooding is that we actually run Engine on top of Engine.

text: So as Engine investigates traces for our go-to-market agents and for our coding agents, it produces traces.

text: And so our team gets notified when our own product is acting up in a little way or something might have failed or there's a suboptimal response in one of the outputs that Engine has.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so it's actually becoming one of the primary ways that we identify opportunities for growth on Engine.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And our team is constantly monitoring this Slack feed of notifications with these issues.

text: I want to highlight a couple of interesting just notes and kind of thoughts that we've had as we have been working on improving Engine, specifically around kind of our use of different models.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Something interesting is that different tasks obviously require different levels of intelligence.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But I have also found that for specific tasks that we run Engine on, using these non-frontier models actually can be more effective.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If it's a quote-unquote dumb task, it's sometimes better to use a dumber or a smaller model as opposed to these state-of-the-art models that are really expensive and really bulky.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we constantly play around with swapping out the models that are used for the different tasks that are handled by Engine.

text: An engine, as it pours through traces, does investigation, it can find multiple traces with that problem, cluster them together based on root cause.

text: But oftentimes, it's difficult to find errors with just a single trace, and there are some kinds of errors that may appear the same at first glance.

text: So let's say between September 1st and September 14th, our team has swapped out a new model for our agent, and we see that the cost and latency are pretty much the same, even though we were expecting to see a huge drop in cost or a huge drop in latency.

text: And if I look at trace A versus trace B, these might look like the exact same thing, and no change is recognizable.

text: This is important for your team to know that some amount of time it's taking an inefficient path that you should be aware of, that you should work to contain.

text: Now, what I've talked about so far,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what we've been asking ourselves since our first launch is how can we actually test for our users?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Right now we create a proposed fix and we hand you the evals and let you experiment on that.

text: But the vision that we have for Engine is the finding of problems, the fixing of those problems, and the testing of that fix all autonomously.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is what we are releasing with our validated fixes as part of Engine.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what I want to do is walk you through how this actually works.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Harrison spoke to this a little bit in the keynote, and I want to get into some of the nitty gritty here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Engine still finds issues as it does today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It finds an issue about tool looping, and it identifies specific inputs that it's seen in production that have broken your agent in some way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now to verify that this problem is real, we actually send those same inputs to your production version of your agent to verify that it is still broken in your production version.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We want to confirm this is an ongoing problem and reproduce the bug as you would in software.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: After we've identified and confirmed this is a real problem, we will then propose a fix and spin that up in a preview branch and in a preview deployment available on our LangSmith deployments platform.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we will run those same breaking inputs against this previewed fix version of your agent so that we can confirm that whatever fix engine has spun up really solves the problem that identified and that those breaking inputs are no longer breaking in this proposed version of your agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And after verifying that this fix is effective for those inputs, we want to look at a broader set of inputs, like the ones that you have in a LangSmith dataset.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so you can configure the different datasets that you have on LangSmith, and so the engine will run evals against the existing inputs that have been breaking your agent, as well as the broader range of inputs that you want to ensure do not regress.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so what you end up with is now much more than a kind of proposed issue and a hint at what you might want to solve and a hint at how you might solve it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And instead you get a verified issue that we know is still breaking your agent and you get a verified fix that we know addresses the problem and does not regress against other examples.
